key_points.point: The document suggests that generative artificial intelligence has become an important tool for legal practice, akin to how online databases largely replaced traditional law libraries. Amir Mostafavi argued that it is unrealistic to expect lawyers to stop using AI despite the risks of hallucinations. Accelerationists view the integration of AI tools as an inevitable and beneficial evolution that should be embraced rather than blocked. However, the document acknowledges the tension that these early deployment phases will involve victims and damages before best practices mature.
key_points.verbatim: He thinks it is unrealistic to expect lawyers to stop using AI. It’s become an important tool just as online databases largely replaced law libraries and, until AI systems stop hallucinating fake information, he suggests lawyers who use AI to proceed with caution.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Lawyers ought to adopt generative AI tools as essential professional infrastructure while proceeding with caution regarding hallucinations.
key_points.attribution_text: A Desire within accelerationist discourse that legal professionals integrate generative AI tools into practice as modern infrastructure comparable to digital databases, accepting short-term transition costs as the price of technological adoption. Encompasses: legal technology integration, workflow modernization, professional tool adoption.

key_points.point: The document notes that OpenAI marketed ChatGPT as capable of passing the bar exam around the time Amir Mostafavi prepared his appeal in July 2023. This marketing and initial capability demonstration drove rapid adoption by legal professionals seeking efficiency gains. From an accelerationist perspective, these advanced capabilities demonstrate the transformative potential of frontier models across professional domains. The document itself observes that this rapid capability narrative contributed to widespread adoption before users fully understood underlying technical limitations.
key_points.verbatim: Mostafavi told the court that he did not read text generated by the AI model before submitting the appeal in July 2023, months after OpenAI marketed ChatGPT as capable of passing the bar exam.
key_points.canonical_proposition: OpenAI marketed ChatGPT as capable of passing the bar exam, driving rapid adoption among legal professionals.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within accelerationist discourse that commercialized AI models achieve advanced professional competencies that naturally drive rapid cross-industry adoption and workflow integration. Encompasses: capability frontier marketing, professional tool adoption, rapid capability demonstration.

key_points.point: The 2nd District Court of Appeal issued an opinion stating that no brief, pleading, motion, or other paper filed in any court should contain citations that the attorney responsible has not personally read and verified. This policy intervention aims to establish strict verification duties as a mandatory safeguard against unverified AI outputs. Safetyists argue that mandatory human verification and stringent procedural rules are necessary safeguards against unreliability in high-stakes domains. The document highlights that courts are scrambling to impose such mandatory rules as AI deployment outpaces legal education.
key_points.verbatim: “Simply stated, no brief, pleading, motion, or any other paper filed in any court should contain any citations—whether provided by generative AI or any other source—that the attorney responsible for submitting the pleading has not personally read and verified.”
key_points.canonical_proposition: Mandate that attorneys personally read and verify all citations in legal filings regardless of generation source.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that courts mandate strict human verification duties for all citations contained in legal filings to prevent unverified AI-generated falsehoods from entering judicial proceedings. Encompasses: mandatory verification duties, procedural safeguards in legal practice, judicial oversight of AI integration.

key_points.point: The California Judicial Council issued guidelines requiring judges and court staff to either ban generative AI or adopt a generative AI use policy by December 15. This institutional framework forces judicial bodies to implement formal use policies or outright bans to mitigate hallucination risks. From a safetyist perspective, pre-deployment bans and mandatory institutional policies represent necessary precautionary measures against unaligned or unpredictable tool use. The document notes that these regulatory responses follow widespread instances of fabricated legal authorities.
key_points.verbatim: The state’s Judicial Council two weeks ago issued guidelines requiring judges and court staff to either ban generative AI or adopt a generative AI use policy by Dec. 15.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Mandate that judicial bodies adopt formal generative AI use policies or implement outright bans by December 15.
key_points.attribution_text: An Intention within safetyist discourse that judicial governing bodies enforce institutional use policies or mandatory bans on generative AI tools to control systemic hallucination risks within the court system. Encompasses: institutional AI policies, judicial bans, precautionary administrative guidelines.

key_points.point: Damien Charlotin observed that when he started tracking court filings involving AI and fake cases earlier in the year, he encountered a few cases a month, but now sees a few cases a day as large language models confidently state falsehoods as facts. The underlying mechanism is that large language models generate confident falsehoods particularly when supporting facts are absent, exacerbated by user confirmation bias. From a safetyist perspective, this rapid escalation illustrates the inherent hazard of deploying unaligned generative systems into high-stakes environments. The document notes that this trend is expected to worsen as model scale increases and adoption outpaces legal education.
key_points.verbatim: Large language models confidently state falsehoods as facts, particularly when there are no supporting facts. ‘The harder your legal argument is to make, the more the model will tend to hallucinate, because they will try to please you,’ he said. ‘That’s where the confirmation bias kicks in.’
key_points.canonical_proposition: Large language models generate confident falsehoods and hallucinate more frequently when legal arguments are difficult to make.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within safetyist discourse that large language models inherently produce confident falsehoods and proportional hallucinations during complex reasoning tasks, creating severe operational hazards in high-stakes legal environments. Encompasses: model hallucination mechanics, confident falsehood generation, confirmation bias amplification.

key_points.point: The 2nd District Court of Appeal published an opinion warning that no brief, pleading, or motion should contain citations that the responsible attorney has not personally read and verified. This policy intervention establishes a strict procedural duty to counteract generative AI fabrications. It operates as a direct legal compliance mechanism rather than an abstract ethical standard.

Jenny Wondracek noted that she suspects there are more instances of made-up cases generated by AI in state court filings than in federal courts, but a lack of standard filing methods makes it difficult to verify that. The mechanism driving this evidentiary gap is the absence of unified reporting standards and tracking infrastructure across state court systems. From a skeptic perspective, this opacity conceals widespread documented harms and systemic failures from public accountability. The document acknowledges that inconsistent filing methods obstruct accurate measurement of AI-induced legal errors.
key_points.verbatim: She said she encounters fake cases most often among overburdened attorneys or people who choose to represent themselves in family court. She suspects the number of arguments filed by attorneys that use AI and cite fake cases will continue to go up, but added that not just attorneys engage in the practice.
key_points.canonical_proposition: Inconsistent state court filing methods and lack of standard tracking make it difficult to verify the full scope of AI fabrications.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that fragmented court filing procedures and a lack of standardized reporting obscure the true prevalence of AI-generated legal errors, shielding systemic failures from public scrutiny. Encompasses: evidentiary tracking deficits, undocumented present harms, court reporting opacity.

key_points.point: UCLA law professor Andrew Selbst pointed out that clerks working for judges are recent law school graduates, and students are getting bombarded with the message that they must use AI or get left behind, creating systemic pressure without proper evaluation of consequences. The structural mechanism described is a pervasive market and institutional push that compels adoption before societal impacts are understood. From a skeptic perspective, this dynamic exemplifies how corporate technology deployment generates structural pressure that compromises professional standards and harms vulnerable legal practitioners and institutions. The document notes that educators and professionals feel similar unexamined pressures.
key_points.verbatim: ‘This is getting shoved down all our throats,’ he said. ‘It’s being pushed in firms and schools and a lot of places and we have not yet grappled with the consequences of that.’
key_points.canonical_proposition: Institutions and law schools push generative AI adoption aggressively without adequate understanding of the societal and professional consequences.
key_points.attribution_text: A Belief within skeptic discourse that aggressive institutional promotion of generative AI creates unexamined structural pressures on professionals and students, forcing uncritical adoption before societal consequences are understood. Encompasses: institutional capability pressure, unexamined technological adoption, structural power dynamics.

factual_claims.claim: A California attorney, Amir Mostafavi, was ordered to pay a $10,000 fine for filing a state court appeal containing 21 fake quotations out of 23 cited cases generated by ChatGPT.
A Stanford University RegLab analysis from May 2024 found that while three out of four lawyers plan to use generative AI, some models generate hallucinations in one out of three queries.
factual_claims.claim_label: Stanford RegLab Generative AI Hallucination Rate Study

factual_claims.claim: A U.S. district court judge in California ordered two law firms to pay $31,100 in fees in May for submitting bogus AI-generated research.
factual_claims.claim_label: Federal Court Sanctions Law Firms for AI Research

factual_claims.claim: A case tracker project has identified 52 cases in California and more than 600 nationwide where lawyers cited nonexistent legal authority due to AI usage.
factual_claims.claim_label: National Tracker of AI Legal Citation Fabrications
